"Temporal" is an adjective with three distinct meanings depending on the context it appears in. Two of those meanings are closely related to each other, and one is completely separate. A learner must know all three to truly understand this word.

This is the most common and fundamental meaning. When something is described as "temporal," it means it belongs to, exists within, or is measured by time. The opposite of temporal in this sense is eternal — meaning something that exists outside of time, forever.

Think of it this way: anything that has a beginning and an end is temporal. Your life is temporal. A conversation is temporal. A season is temporal. But the concept of infinity, or God in religious thinking, is considered eternal — the very opposite.

Examples:

  • "The temporal sequence of events was hard to follow." — meaning the order of events in time.
  • "Humans are temporal beings." — meaning we exist within time; we are born and we die.
  • "The film uses temporal shifts to tell the story." — meaning the film jumps back and forth in time.
  • "Temporal distance makes memories feel less painful." — meaning the passage of time softens pain.

This meaning is very common in philosophy, science, film, and literature. Whenever you see "temporal" used alongside words like sequence, order, shift, gap, distance, awareness, or pattern, it is almost always this meaning at work.
Meaning 2 — Relating to Worldly, Non-Religious Affairs

This meaning is closely linked to Meaning 1, and here's the logical connection: things that belong to time are things that belong to this world — because this world exists in time, while spiritual or divine things are considered to exist beyond time. So "temporal" came to describe anything secular, earthly, and non-spiritual, as opposed to what is sacred, divine, or religious.

This meaning appears most often in history, politics, law, and religion, especially when discussing the relationship between church and state.

Examples:

  • "The king held temporal power, while the Pope held spiritual power." — meaning the king ruled over earthly, political life, while the Pope ruled over souls and religious life.
  • "Temporal courts deal with civil and criminal matters, not moral ones." — meaning secular courts, not religious ones.
  • "She gave up her temporal possessions to enter the monastery." — meaning she gave up her worldly belongings — property, money, material things.
  • "The bishop's temporal authority was eventually stripped away." — meaning his power over land and politics (not his religious role) was taken.

So in this meaning, "temporal" = of this world, not of the divine. Its opposites here are words like spiritual, sacred, divine, ecclesiastical.
Meaning 3 — Relating to the Temples of the Head

This is a completely separate meaning with no connection to time or worldly affairs. In anatomy and medicine, "temporal" refers to the temples — the flat regions on the sides of your skull, just beside and slightly above your eyes. The word simply describes that part of the human head.

Examples:

  • "The temporal lobe is the region of the brain located near your temples." — The temporal lobe handles memory, language understanding, and processing sound.
  • "He suffered a temporal bone fracture." — a break in the bone forming the side of the skull.
  • "The temporal artery runs along the side of the head." — a blood vessel in that region. A condition called temporal arteritis is an inflammation of this artery.

Whenever you see "temporal" used in a medical or anatomical context — especially alongside words like lobe, bone, artery, cortex — it always means this: the side of the head.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context will almost always make it obvious:

  • Medical or anatomical context → it's about the temples of the head.
  • Historical, political, or religious context → it's about worldly vs. spiritual matters.
  • Philosophical, scientific, or everyday context involving time, sequence, or duration → it's about time.

The word "temporal" is not a word you'd typically use in casual everyday speech. It belongs to formal, academic, medical, or intellectual writing and discussion. So when you encounter it in a book, article, or lecture, pause and ask: Is this about time? About worldly vs. spiritual power? Or about the human skull? The answer will almost always be immediately clear from what surrounds the word.
